ov_intro: Outside companies send us customer records (an ID, a name, an email). This system receives those records, saves them into our customer table, and gives operators screens to watch the work happen and fix anything that gets stuck.
ov_flow: A sender drops a letter in the mailbox — a third party calls our API.
The clerk stamps it received — the API stores an ingest record and answers accepted within a fraction of a second. The sender never waits for delivery.
A courier delivers it immediately — the fast-lane worker writes the customer into the customer table, usually in under a second.
Every 2 minutes a supervisor checks for letters nobody picked up — the sweeper re-queues anything the courier missed.
Once a night an auditor counts everything — aggregate-stats records totals for the Overview page.

ov_guar.t: Every accepted request is stored first. Every accepted request ends as DONE or FAILED — never silently dropped.
If two updates for the same customer race, the newer request wins and the older one is skipped as stale.

ov_words: The current truth: one row per externalId with name and email.
One accepted request, with a status: PENDING, PROCESSING, DONE, FAILED.
A waiting line of jobs. customer-fast-lane = deliver now, customer-cron = scheduled work.
One unit of work in a queue (for example: process one ingest row).
Work on a schedule: the 2-minute sweeper and the nightly stats.
A history entry saying a job finished or failed, with how long it took.
ov_run_1: starts everything. Fixed ports: dashboard on
ov_health: Open the real Overview first whenever something feels wrong. If PENDING or FAILED is growing, go to Ingests. If failed jobs are growing, go to Queues. If a card says unavailable (Redis down?), the queue system is unreachable — the inbox cards still work.
cu_what: What it is: the truth the whole system maintains. Seeded with 300,000 demo rows (EXT-000001 …). 50 rows per page so it stays fast.
cu_use: Type an exact customer ID (for example EXT-000001) or the start of an email (for example eloise) and press Search. Flip pages with Prev/Next.
cu_test: Search a short email prefix → a list.
qu_what: What it is: the waiting lines, both lanes. Pick a lane (fast-lane or cron) and a job state (waiting, active, delayed, completed, failed) and page through the jobs. Each row shows the job id, name, how many attempts it took, and — for failed jobs — the failure reason.
qu_use: When the Overview shows failed jobs, select fast-lane + failed, read the failedReason, fix the underlying cause, then press Retry on the job. Retry only works while the job is still stored; if it says not found, the job aged out and you should requeue the inbox row from Ingests instead.
qu_test: Create a customer with name __FAIL__boom through the API (a deliberate poison used for training). Within ~10 seconds it appears under failed with reason injected fault. Press Retry → it runs again and fails again, proving retries execute.
qu_push_h: Where jobs come from (no HTTP to the worker)
qu_push: Nobody calls the worker over HTTP. The API pushes with queue.add() and the worker's @Processor picks the job up. The contract is three things: the same queue-name string, the same Redis host/port, and .add() on one side with process() on the other. BullModule.forRoot plus registerQueue alone only open the Redis connection — without a producer and a processor, nothing ever moves.
qu_push_steps: Wire it: BullModule.forRoot({ connection: redisConnection() }) opens Redis; BullModule.registerQueue({ name }) hands out a queue handle. Both processes do this: apps/api/src/api.module.ts and apps/worker/src/worker.module.ts, with the names shared from packages/shared/src/index.ts.

Push it: CustomersService.accept stores the PENDING inbox row first, then calls fastLane.add('process-ingest', { ingestId }, { ...FAST_LANE_JOB_OPTS, jobId }) — apps/api/src/customers/customers.service.ts:43-47. The add is raced against a 3s timeout because BullMQ buffers instead of throwing when Redis is down.
Consume it: @Processor('customer-fast-lane') plus process(job) in apps/worker/src/fast-lane.processor.ts:13-25. Attempts and backoff come from FAST_LANE_JOB_OPTS (attempts 3, exponential backoff 2s).

Fresh NestJS checklist: npm i @nestjs/bullmq bullmq, forRoot + registerQueue in the module, an InjectQueue(...).add(jobName, data, opts) producer, and a @Processor(name) class extending WorkerHost with process(job). If producer and consumer live in different processes, both need forRoot + registerQueue pointed at the same Redis.
qu_redis: Redis down stalls both lanes: the queues are Redis keys (bull:customer-fast-lane:*), so .add() buffers and process() never fires. The API still returns 202 ACCEPTED — the PENDING row is already in Postgres — the inbox pages keep working, and the sweeper re-enqueues missed rows once Redis returns.
cr_sched_h: Who creates the schedules (the worker itself)
cr_sched: The two cron rows are not seeded data. SchedulerService registers them with upsertJobScheduler on every worker boot — idempotent, so restarts never duplicate them — and the CronProcessor consumes them on the customer-cron lane.
cr_sched_steps: Register: apps/worker/src/scheduler.service.ts:16-27 — upsertJobScheduler('sweep-pending', { pattern: '*/2 * * * *' }) and upsertJobScheduler('aggregate-stats', { pattern: '0 2 * * *' }).

Run: @Processor('customer-cron') plus process(job) in apps/worker/src/cron.processor.ts:28-44 switches on job.name — sweepPending() re-enqueues stuck rows with fastLane.addBulk, aggregateStats() writes the nightly counts.

Trigger now skips the wait: the dashboard calls the admin trigger endpoint (same job name, run immediately) — the proof still lands on Logs and the Cron page, never in the trigger response beyond a job id.
cr_what: What it is: the two schedules — sweep-pending (every 2 minutes) and aggregate-stats (nightly 02:00) — with their pattern, timezone, and the result of their last run.
cr_use: Press Trigger now (you get a confirmation dialog) to run a schedule immediately instead of waiting. Use it after an outage: trigger sweep-pending and watch PENDING rows get picked up. Do not trigger repeatedly — one run is enough; duplicates are harmless but noisy.
cr_test: Press Trigger now on aggregate-stats, confirm, wait a few seconds, reload: its last result updates with fresh customer totals, and a new COMPLETED row appears on the Logs page.
in_what: What it is: the inbox — every accepted request and its status. Filter by status. Each row shows the customer ID, whether it was a CREATE or UPDATE, the attempt count, and the error text when it failed.
in_use_h: How to use it (main recovery tool)
in_use: One stuck row → Requeue sends it back to the fast lane.
Many failed rows → Requeue all failed sends every recoverable FAILED row back at once.
Requeueing a DONE row is safe: the worker sees it is already done and skips it.
in_test: Filter FAILED → find the __FAIL__boom row with its error text. Press Requeue → it runs again (and fails again until the cause is fixed, which is the point: the loop is visible and controllable). This page keeps working even when Redis is down.
lo_what: What it is: the history of everything workers did — which queue, which job, COMPLETED or FAILED, attempts used, duration, error, and finish time. Filter by queue and status. Read-only: nothing here can be clicked to change anything, which makes it safe for auditing.
lo_test: Trigger a cron job, requeue a row, or retry a job, then filter Logs — a matching row appears within seconds. Filter customer-fast-lane + FAILED to see every failed delivery attempt.
wt_steps: Send a customer through the API (replace the ID to repeat): POST /create-customer with externalId EXT-990001, name Ada, email ada@example.com and header x-api-key dev-key-1. You get an ingestId, status ACCEPTED, and delayMs.
Open Ingests, filter PENDING — your row appears, then flips to DONE within a second (or after the configured delay — see training tip below).
Open Customers, search EXT-990001 — Ada is there.
Send an update for the same ID with a new name. Customers shows one row with the new name — newest wins.
Open Logs — one COMPLETED run for your ingest.
